tldr: Pollack, founder of Spring AI, applies the feedback loop from control theory to coding agents: define success, judge with evidence, read the agent's session log, change one variable, repeat.
summary: Pollack opens with the questions enterprises ask of any agent: is it working, how would I know, can it be cheaper, am I locked in? 'The agent said it's done' is no answer. Citing Andrew Ng on disciplined evals, he frames an edit-compile loop for AI. His example is a JetBrains developer advocate's spec-driven Pet Clinic feature using Timefold: seven use cases written as EARS requirements plus RFC 2119 architectural rules. The agent produced 290 tests in about 20 minutes, yet evaluation found a lock-ordering violation and most architectural rules failing.

The evaluation comes from his Agent Judge library, with a JUnit and AssertJ-style API. Judges return judgments (pass, fail, inconclusive, not applicable), juries of judges return verdicts, and reports carry the evidence: line numbers and tests, not a boolean. Judges can run on any agentic CLI or Java framework; numeric scores, he says, are meaningless. Under a 'principle of least intelligence' he prefers deterministic tools, and bundled PMD, JaCoCo, mutation testing, Error Prone, Lincheck, ArchUnit, SpotBugs, NullAway and complexity metrics into a skill that configures them on a brownfield codebase and drives findings to zero, trying it on the Java MCP SDK.

Attention is limited: one skill asked to raise coverage and adopt new Spring testing utilities ignored the second goal. Hence a workflow engine mixing deterministic and AI steps, branching on verdicts, with steps swappable as DI beans; he uses it to triage open-source PRs. Agent Client puts one API over any agentic CLI, so switching model or provider is configuration, and he advises calling an existing CLI before building a harness. The stop criterion is cost per verified result: prove the task on the biggest model, then step down while quality holds, and finally freeze the evals into a benchmark (Agent Bench, inspired by Terminal-Bench).

'Reading the agent's diary' means classifying every tool call in the session log. A refined prompt cut a coverage run from 86 to 60 calls at nearly the same cost ($3.60 versus $3.46), and repeated 10-15-call JaCoCo parsing became a candidate tool. Planning artifacts live in a separate 'steward' Git repository bound to one or more code repos. A judge run against the ACP spec found a missed 'must' in his own, well-tested ACP Java SDK. His closing warning: keep business logic out of vendor agent workflows, because the system should run the model, not the reverse.
keyPoints: An agent-built Pet Clinic feature with 290 tests passed 51 of 52 behavioural criteria, but evaluation surfaced a lock-ordering bug and most of the 13 architectural rules failing.

Agent Judge: judges produce judgments, juries of judges produce verdicts, and reports carry the evidence. Outcomes include inconclusive and not applicable, and Pollack considers numeric scores meaningless.

Principle of least intelligence: lean on deterministic tools (ArchUnit, PMD, NullAway, Lincheck, mutation testing, cognitive complexity) because a number gives the agent a real signal to iterate against.
Split work into focused steps; a single skill asked to add coverage and adopt new Spring testing utilities ignored the second goal.
Agent Client is one Java API over many agentic CLIs, making the model or harness a configuration change inside a workflow of deterministic and AI steps.
Performance index: total cost of all attempts divided by verified acceptable results. Start with the biggest model, then step down while quality holds.
Session-log analysis (tool-call categories, transition heat maps) showed a refined prompt cut calls from 86 to 60 with almost no cost difference ($3.60 vs $3.46).
A separate 'steward' Git repository holds project knowledge, plans and evals so they outlive any CLI or model and don't pollute the codebase.
takeaways: Write requirements in a structured form (EARS or RFC 2119 must/shall) so a judge can check the agent's output against each one with evidence.
Wire ArchUnit, mutation testing, NullAway and complexity metrics into the build and hand the agent the report to drive to zero.
Read your agent's session logs and turn repeated multi-call chores, such as parsing a JaCoCo report, into tools.
Measure cost per verified result on the strongest model first, then try cheaper models against the same evals, changing one variable at a time.
Keep workflow logic in your own code rather than a vendor's agent workflow feature to avoid lock-in.

quotes.text: Show me evidence. Just don't tell me.
It's not that the model is running the system, it's the other way around. Our system is running the model.

watchIf: You let coding agents produce real code and want a concrete, Java-centric method to verify their output and compare models on cost and quality.
